title: A Rare Presentation of Coinfection: Dengue Virus and Hepatitis A Virus
case_text:
A 34-year-old previously healthy male presented with high grade fever associated with constitutional symptoms of five days' duration. He was complaining of right hypochondrium pain and tea-coloured urine for two days associated with yellowish discolouration of the eyes. He had severe loss of appetite to food and water, but his bowel habits had been normal throughout the illness. On admission, he was afebrile with normal vital signs but was deeply icteric. His abdominal examination revealed a tender, mild hepatomegaly while his cardiovascular, respiratory, and nervous system examination was normal.
His full blood count revealed a white cell count of 3 x 103 muL with a platelet count of 116 x 103 muL. His aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were 5162 U/L and 3964 U/L, respectively. Initial total bilirubin was found to be 61.7 mumol/L with an increased direct fraction. His prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (PT/INR) and serum protein were normal throughout the illness. His dengue IgM antibody done by chromatographic immunoassay was positive on the 6th day of the illness. Hepatitis A IgM antibody done by the ELISA technique was positive on day 6 of the illness, while hepatitis A IgG antibody was negative. Other investigations done during the hospital stay are summarized in Table 1.
During the course of the illness, the patient was closely monitored for features of development of liver failure while continuing with the precritical monitoring of the dengue fever. The patient's hospital stay was uneventful, and he did not develop features of acute liver failure or features of plasma leakage as in DHF. He was discharged on day 10 of the illness. On follow-up, his AST, ALT, and bilirubin have become normal.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Dengue
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: coinfection of dengue fever and acute hepatitis A
